title: Queen against rook I: the Philidor position
summary: The position where the rook has to leave its king, and the fork that punishes every escape.
step.intro: Queen against rook is a win, but the queen cannot do it alone: a rook glued to its king defends everything. The secret is a position Philidor studied in 1777, and the whole endgame heads towards it. Look closely: black king on the edge, rook next to it, our king on c6 a knight's move from the black king, and the queen on a5. It is Black to move, and that is Black's problem. The king has nowhere to go: a7 and a8 belong to the queen, c7 to our king. So the rook will have to move.
step.near: First, the rook moves that lose at once. On a7, the queen mates on d8. On c7 or d7, the rook is captured. On b6, b5 and b4 as well: the king or the queen takes it. In other words, the rook has no square near its king. What is left is the king move to c8 and the escapes far away.
step.pin: The black king went to c8 and let go of the rook. Only the king defends it. Attack it in a way that leaves it unable to move.
step.pin.hint: A square on the a-file from which the queen attacks b7 and still holds the rook in front of its king.
step.pin.done: The rook was pinned: if it left b7, the king would be in check. That is why the king move does not save Black.
step.far: Now the escapes far away: the marked squares. This is where the endgame is won. Far from its king the rook is loose, and a loose rook falls to a fork: a series of checks ending with the queen attacking king and rook at the same time. The rule is short. The first check is almost always on e5. From there the queen looks down the long diagonal, the file and the rank, and picks the next check according to where the rook is.
step.fork: The rook ran to g7. Give the check on e5 and see what the queen attacks from there.
step.fork.hint: Qe5+: the queen checks along the diagonal and, on the same diagonal, on the other side, stands the rook on g7.
step.fork.done: A fork. The same check on e5 picks up the rook on b2, along the long diagonal. Two squares solved with one move.
step.efile: The rook went to e7. Now the check on e5 fails: the rook takes the queen. Find the other check that attacks the rook.
step.efile.hint: A check on the b-file, on a square that is also on the diagonal of e7.
step.efile.done: It is the only exception to the rule: with the rook on the e-file, the check is on b4.
step.ladder: Rook on h7, as far as it can go along the rank. One check is not enough. Climb the ladder: e5, then the corner a1, then b1. At the end the queen looks at h7 along the diagonal.
step.ladder.hint: Qe5+, Qa1+ and Qb1+. From b1, the b1-h7 diagonal reaches the rook.
step.ladder.done: Three checks and the rook falls. Notice the black king never had a choice: check after check.
step.rf7: Rook on f7. Three checks again, and the queen stays on the e-file: e5, e3 and, last, the back-rank square that attacks king and rook.
step.rf7.hint: Qe5+, then Qe3+ and Qe8+. From e8 the queen checks along the rank and attacks f7.
step.rf7.done: Another square solved. If you prefer, start with the check on b4 and go on via a3 and b3: it comes to the same.
step.rb1: The most stubborn defence: the rook goes to b1, as far as possible. It takes four checks. Start on e5, drop to d4, go to the corner h8 and finish on h7, from where the queen looks at b1.
step.rb1.hint: Qe5+, Qd4+, Qh8+ and Qh7+. The h7-b1 diagonal is the one that wins the rook.
step.rb1.done: That is the longest line of the Philidor position, and you have just played it. If the rook goes to b3 the idea is the same, with the queen on g7 and g8: you will see it in the exercises.
step.white: And what if, in this same position, it is our move? Then the zugzwang is ours: any move spoils the position. The way out is to lose a tempo. The queen draws a triangle, e5, a1 and back to a5, with two checks on the way. The position is identical, only with Black to move.
step.triangle: Pass the move to Black. Three queen moves: e5 with check, a1 with check, and a5.
step.triangle.hint: Qe5+, the king goes to a8 or a7; Qa1+, the king returns to b8; Qa5.
step.triangle.done: The same position, and now Black is to move. Remember this triangle: it turns up throughout the queen against rook endgame.
step.squeeze: A warning. Once you have the Philidor position, do not try to squeeze harder. Here the queen went to a6 and the king to b6, and Black plays the rook to c6 with check. If the king takes, the black king is stalemated. If the queen takes, the same. And if the king runs, the checks go on. A draw. Averbakh shows this trap, and it holds for the whole endgame: a queen too close to the cornered king smells of stalemate.
step.false: Another warning: the false Philidor. It looks like the same position, but our king is on a6, not c6. That changes everything: now the rook has the square d7, far from our king, and c7 is not guarded. It is still a win, but it takes more than twice as many moves. The right king stands on c6, a knight's move from the black king.
step.recap: What to take away. One: Philidor is king on c6, queen on a5, black rook and king on the edge; with Black to move, the rook falls. Two: if it is our move, the triangle e5, a1, a5 passes the move. Three: a loose rook is punished with checks until the fork, and the first check is on e5, except with the rook on the e-file. And do not squeeze harder than that.
step.finish: Your turn, against the machine, and it defends well. This is the Philidor position with you to move: pass the move, see where the rook runs and find the fork. After winning the rook, give the king and queen mate.
ex.e01: White to move. It is the Philidor position, but it is your move. What is the first move?
ex.e01.hint: You need to hand back the same position with Black to move. Start the triangle.
ex.e01.solution: Qe5+ (Qd5 makes the same triangle the other way round). Then the queen goes to the corner with check and returns to a5: the position is the same and Black is to move.
ex.e02: White to move. The rook ran to b2. Win it in two moves.
ex.e02.hint: The first check of the rule. From there the long diagonal reaches b2.
ex.e02.solution: Qe5+ and, wherever the king goes, Qxb2. The queen on e5 checks and attacks the rook along the diagonal.
ex.e03: White to move. The rook is on e7. Which check wins the rook?
ex.e03.hint: On e5 the queen would be captured. Look for the check on the b-file.
ex.e03.solution: Qb4+. The queen checks on the b-file and attacks e7 along the diagonal. Qd8+ also wins the rook, along the back rank.
ex.e04: White to move. The black king stepped out to c8 and the rook stayed on b7. How do you win?
ex.e04.hint: The rook has a single defender, and it stands behind the rook.
ex.e04.solution: Qa6. The rook is pinned against the king and cannot move; next move the queen takes on b7.
ex.e05: White to move. The Philidor position in the other corner, with you to move. Pass the move to Black.
ex.e05.hint: The same triangle, mirrored: a check on the diagonal, a check in the corner and the queen back again.
ex.e05.solution: Qd5+, Qh1+ and Qh5. It is the triangle from the lesson seen from the other side of the board: the position repeats with Black to move.
ex.e06: White to move. The rook went to h7. Three checks win the rook.
ex.e06.hint: The ladder: e5, the corner a1, and the square from which a diagonal reaches h7.
ex.e06.solution: Qe5+, Qa1+ and Qb1+. From b1 the queen checks and attacks h7 along the diagonal: a fork.
ex.e07: White to move. The rook is on f7. Win it with three checks, this time along the b-file and the a-file.
ex.e07.hint: Qb4+ first. Then the queen drops one square along the diagonal and returns to the b-file, with an eye on f7.
ex.e07.solution: Qb4+, Qa3+ and Qb3+. From b3 the diagonal reaches f7. The route via e5, e3 and e8, the one from the lesson, wins in the same number of moves.
ex.e08: White to move. You squeezed too hard with the queen and the rook gave check. Where does the king go?
ex.e08.hint: On b6 the king seems to stay close, but look at the rook check on c6 and count the black king's squares.
ex.e08.solution: Kd6 (or Kd5, or Kb5). On b6, the rook would check on c6 and any capture would stalemate the black king. Away from the rook the win is still there, only longer.
ex.e09: White to move. The rook went to b3. Find the series of checks that wins it.
ex.e09.hint: Start on e5. The final square is g8: from there the queen looks at b3.
ex.e09.solution: Qe5+, Qg7+, Qg8+ and the rook falls on b3. The queen climbs the kingside to the g8-b3 diagonal.
ex.e10: White to move. The most stubborn defence: rook on b1. Four checks, and the last one attacks the rook.
ex.e10.hint: e5, d4, the corner h8 and the square next to it. The diagonal that matters is the one ending on b1.
ex.e10.solution: Qe5+, Qd4+, Qh8+ and Qh7+. From h7 the queen checks along the rank and attacks b1 along the diagonal. It is the longest line of the Philidor position.
key.black: The Philidor position (1777) with Black to move: zugzwang. The king has no square and the rook, wherever it goes, falls to a fork. Diagram from Wikipedia.
key.white: The same position with White to move: the queen draws the triangle e5, a1, a5 and hands the move back.
key.corner: Philidor in the other corner, as in NM BXMSChess's Lichess study. The endgame can finish in any of the four corners.
key.draw: The trap for those who squeeze too hard: the rook checks on c6 and any capture is stalemate. A draw. Wikipedia quotes it from Averbakh.
history: Philidor analysed this position in 1777, and for two centuries the queen against rook endgame was thought to be simple. In December 1978 Ken Thompson, of Bell Labs, finished the first complete database of the endgame and challenged grandmaster Walter Browne, several times United States champion, to win with the queen in fifty moves against the computer Belle. Browne bet a hundred dollars, said half an hour would be enough, and failed. He studied, asked for a rematch and won the rook on exactly the fiftieth move. Since then the endgame has been taken seriously: Svidler, at the 2001 World Championship, let Gelfand escape by the fifty-move rule, and Morozevich, in Pamplona in 2006, fell into a stalemate against Jakovenko. With perfect play the rook falls in at most 31 moves.
practice: Now against the clock, or without it. The position is almost Philidor's: you only need to put the pieces in place and pass the move. The rest you already know.
